title: Designing workflow tools that preserve context
summary: Practical ways to help teams capture incoming work, see what changed, and resume a task without reconstructing every decision.
bodyHtml:
A workflow tool earns its place when it helps someone return to a task and understand what needs attention. That matters in teams where meetings, messages, and new requests regularly interrupt planned work.

Make the first useful action easy

Capturing a request should take less effort than keeping it in your head. Start with enough information to recognize the work later: what came in, who needs it, and a short note about the next step. More detail can follow when the request becomes clearer.

Requiring a complete specification at the moment of capture encourages people to postpone recording the work. A short entry that can be refined is often more useful than an elaborate form left empty.

Keep decisions with the work

A task title rarely explains why a priority changed or what is blocking progress. Notes, recent activity, and a visible next action can give someone a place to restart. The useful question is whether the record helps them continue without searching through several conversations.

Show the state of the day

Views of current priorities and recent activity help people distinguish work that is moving from work that is waiting. A calendar can provide another way to recall when something happened, alongside a list of tasks.

I prefer tools that make these details easy to find and update. The design should reduce the effort of maintaining context throughout an ordinary working day.
